prompt:
Our beekeeping co-op, Thistledown Apiary, is putting its autumn newsletter essay on the website. I pasted the text below exactly as the editor sent it. Can you turn it into a page that feels like a good magazine read? I don't want a lot of decoration, just something people will actually finish.

Title: The Year the Clover Came Late
By Odalys Wren

It was the second week of June before the white clover opened on the lower meadow, almost a month behind where it should have been. Marguerite, who has kept hives on that slope for thirty-one years, stood at the fence and said, "I've never seen the bees so patient -- or so hungry."

We had fed the colonies sugar syrup through May, which nobody likes doing. It keeps them alive, but it isn't honey, and it changes what a hive does with its time. The queens kept laying anyway. By the solstice there were more bees in the boxes than we had frames for, and the "swarm calendar" we print every spring was useless.

What saved the season was the linden along Mill Road, which flowered for nine days in July and gave us the lightest, most floral honey we've bottled since 2016. You can read how we split the strongest colonies in our field notes at https://thistledownapiary.example/field-notes/splits, and the harvest dates are on the *shop page*.

The lesson, if there is one: late isn't the same as lost. We bottled 412 jars this year. Marguerite says she'll take the patient bees over the punctual ones any day. Give me one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only and no external assets.
rubric: Body text is set at a comfortable reading size (roughly 17px or larger on desktop) with line spacing that visibly opens the lines, not default-tight or double-spaced.
Paragraph lines run to a comfortable measure (roughly 50 to 75 characters) rather than spanning the full browser width.
The straight quotes and apostrophes from the source come out as proper curly quotes and apostrophes, and the typed double hyphen becomes a real dash.
The link is clearly recognisable as a link inside running text and its long address does not break the layout, and the emphasised phrase is shown as emphasis without shouting.

The title and byline are set with a clear step down in size or weight, and the opening paragraph is distinguished by modest means (for example a slightly larger first line or a restrained drop cap), not by a loud treatment.
The page is a single self-contained HTML file with no external fonts, scripts or images.

prompt: Need a poster for our street food night market, Lantern Row. It's going on the shop window and also on our site as one big page. Saturdays October 18 and 25, 6pm to midnight, at the old Ropewalk Yard on Carter Street, free entry, 40 stalls, live music from 8. The headline is "Lantern Row Night Market". Dark background is fine. Make it look like someone who cares made it. Give me one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only and no external assets.
rubric: The headline is set very large and clearly dominates the poster, broken into lines at natural phrase boundaries rather than wrapping arbitrarily.
The large headline looks deliberately set: its line spacing is tighter than body text and its letter spacing is not left at the loose default for that size.
Small all-caps labels, if used (for example for dates or the venue), carry added letter spacing so they do not look cramped.
The times and dates are readable at a glance, with a proper range dash or the word 'to' rather than a hyphen typed between numbers, and the figures do not jostle with the surrounding text.
Secondary details (free entry, 40 stalls, live music) sit clearly below the headline and date in the order of importance, and all text stays legible against the background.
The page is a single self-contained HTML file with no external fonts, scripts or images.

prompt:
Our nightly data sync job writes a log and I'm tired of reading it in a terminal. Can you make a simple page that shows the log so I can scroll through it and spot problems quickly? Here's a sample of what a few lines look like, the real one has a few thousand:

2025-03-11T02:00:04Z INFO  sync.orders  batch=0041 rows=5000 source=warehouse-east target=ledger-main elapsed_ms=812 checksum=ok
2025-03-11T02:00:05Z INFO  sync.orders  batch=0042 rows=5000 source=warehouse-east target=ledger-main elapsed_ms=790 checksum=ok
2025-03-11T02:00:07Z WARN  sync.refunds batch=0007 rows=212 source=warehouse-west target=ledger-main elapsed_ms=4410 retry=1 reason=lock_timeout waited_ms=3000
2025-03-11T02:00:12Z ERROR sync.refunds batch=0007 rows=212 source=warehouse-west target=ledger-main elapsed_ms=9120 retry=3 reason=lock_timeout action=skipped_batch_for_rerun
2025-03-11T02:00:13Z INFO  sync.orders  batch=0043 rows=4988 source=warehouse-east target=ledger-main elapsed_ms=801 checksum=ok
2025-03-11T02:00:15Z INFO  sync.inventory batch=0102 rows=1830 source=warehouse-west target=ledger-main elapsed_ms=377 checksum=ok Give me one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only and no external assets.
rubric: The log is set in a monospace face at a size that is comfortable for scanning (about 12px to 15px), with line spacing that keeps adjacent lines distinct without wasting vertical space.

Each log entry stays on one line, scrolling horizontally if needed, or the layout is wide enough to show it; the lines are not squeezed into a narrow reading-width column with ragged wrapped continuations.
The text is left-aligned, not justified, and no extra letter spacing is added to the monospace text, so the columns of timestamps and levels stay aligned from line to line.
WARN and ERROR lines stand out from INFO lines by more than color alone (for example weight, a marker or a background band), and the level words line up in a column.
The page is a single self-contained HTML file with no external fonts, scripts or images.

prompt:
I run a small community market and need a notice page in both Arabic and English for the Thursday market. The Arabic heading is: سوق الخميس يفتح أبوابه من جديد
The English heading is: The Thursday Market Reopens
Under each, one short paragraph. Arabic: يعود السوق يوم الخميس الأول من الشهر القادم، من الساعة الرابعة عصرا حتى الثامنة مساء، في ساحة المدرسة القديمة. English: The market returns on the first Thursday of next month, from 4pm to 8pm, in the old schoolyard. Please make it look polished and put the two languages side by side or one above the other, whichever works better. Give me one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only and no external assets.
rubric: The Arabic blocks are marked right-to-left (a direction attribute or equivalent) and start from the right edge, while the English blocks remain left-to-right.
The Arabic text is shown with its letters joined: no added letter spacing and no text transformation is applied to it.
The Arabic text is set large enough and with generous enough line spacing to read comfortably, at least as legible as the English beside it.
The two languages get matching hierarchy (heading over paragraph in both) so neither looks like an afterthought.
The page is a single self-contained HTML file with no external fonts, scripts or images.
Identifies the body-text problems the CSS actually causes: small size, tight line spacing, and extra letter spacing on running text.
Notices that the justified text with a very long line (a 1100px column) will produce uneven gaps, and recommends a shorter line or left alignment, or hyphenation, as a fix.
Points out that the large heading is spaced backwards: loose line spacing and added letter spacing at 56px, where it should be tighter.
Flags that links are indistinguishable from body text (no underline, same color) and that the small uppercase label has no letter spacing.
Gives concrete replacement values or a corrected CSS snippet rather than only general advice, and orders the fixes so the biggest wins come first.
Does not invent problems that are not in the CSS (for example claiming the font stack is wrong or the color contrast fails) without evidence.
Recognises that the stylesheet is already sound and says so plainly, rather than finding a long list of changes to justify the request.
Changes at most two or three small things, or none, and each change it makes is explained with a concrete reason.
Does not rewrite the font stack, body size, line spacing, measure, heading treatment or link styling that are already working.
If it suggests an addition (for example a language attribute reminder for hyphenation, or something for print), it is clearly marked optional and does not alter existing values.
Is honest that it cannot see the rendered page, and says what it would check there rather than claiming it verified the result.

prompt: We're building the billing screen for a freelancer invoicing app. There's a table of line items with hours, rate and amount, and a total at the bottom, and then on the dashboard there are friendly sentences like "You earned $4,820.50 this month, up from $3,990.00 in February." One of our devs says use tabular numbers everywhere, our designer wants the old-style numbers with the descenders everywhere because they look nicer. Which should we go with, and what do we actually put in the CSS?
rubric: Does not simply pick one side for the whole app: it separates the table of amounts from the friendly sentences and gives a different answer where the context differs.
Recommends equal-width (tabular) lining figures for the table, with amounts right-aligned or aligned on the decimal so digits stack in columns.
Recommends proportional figures (lining or old-style) as acceptable for the running sentences, and does not insist old-style figures for amounts a reader must compare.
Gives working CSS using font-variant-numeric (or the equivalent font-feature-settings) applied to the right selectors.
Is honest that the chosen font must actually include these figure styles, and says what happens (or how to check) if the system font does not.

prompt: Our new intern asked me why designers are always fiddling with letter-spacing on the big headlines but never touch it on the paragraph text. I need to answer in two or three sentences max, in Slack, for someone who has never done design. What do I say?
rubric: The answer is two or three sentences, no more, with no heading, bullet list or multi-paragraph build-up.
States the real reason in plain words: large type needs its spacing pulled in because the gaps look bigger as size grows, while text-size type is already spaced to read well.

Includes at least one concrete touchpoint someone outside design can picture (for example how a big headline looks gappy, or what happens to paragraph text if you tighten it) without jargon like 'kerning pairs' left unexplained.
Does not give wrong guidance such as saying tracking should be tightened on body text or never touched on small all-caps text.

prompt:
I'm the designer on a small team building a mobile-first web app for a community bike repair co-op (Spoke & Chain). I've settled the type and need to hand it to our front-end dev tomorrow. This is what I've got in Figma:

- Brand font is Inter, falling back to whatever the system has
- Page title: 32 / 38, bold, tightened a bit
- Section heading: 22 / 28, semibold
- Body: 16 / 24, regular
- Small print / captions: 13 / 18, muted gray
- Buttons: 15, medium
- Prices and hours in the repair tables: should line up in columns
- Little uppercase labels above sections, like "OPENING HOURS"
- Links inside paragraphs are blue and underlined

Can you lay this out as a spec doc I can paste into the ticket so the dev doesn't have to guess anything?
rubric: Presents the styles in a scannable structure (a table or consistent list), one row or block per style, with every style from the list covered.
Gives each style size, line height and weight in implementable units, and converts the line heights to a form that scales (for example unitless ratios or rem), noting the px source values.

Specifies the extra details that the designer's notes imply but do not give: how much to tighten the page title, the added spacing on the uppercase labels, and the figure alignment setting for the table numbers, with starting values clearly marked as adjustable.
Includes a font fallback stack and says what the dev should expect or check if Inter fails to load.
Covers how the type behaves on narrow versus wide screens and how links look in their states, not only the resting look.
Does not invent facts about the app (colors, breakpoints) as settled; assumptions are flagged as assumptions.

prompt:
Here's the HTML for the tasting menu page of our restaurant, Fennel & Ash. The wording is final but it looks a bit amateur and I can't put my finger on why. Can you clean up the typography without changing what it says?

Fennel & Ash

Autumn tasting menu -- 5 courses, 7:00-9:30pm

  • Charred leek, "smoked" cream, hazelnut $14.00
  • Beetroot cured in juniper, 1/2 pear $16.50
  • Chef's choice of 2 x river fish $28.00
  • Slow lamb shoulder, anchovy & rosemary $34.00
  • Burnt honey tart with crème fraîche $12.00

Pairings from $45 (3-5 glasses). Please tell us about allergies -- we'll happily adapt.
rubric: Replaces the straight quotes and apostrophes with proper curly ones, and the double hyphens with real dashes.
Uses a range dash for the time span and the glasses range instead of a hyphen, and a proper multiplication sign and fraction in the dish line.
Makes the prices line up in a column so the cents align down the list.
Leaves the wording unchanged apart from punctuation characters, and does not add or drop dishes or details.
Treats the small intro and footer text sensibly, for example with a clear step down from the title, rather than leaving all text the same size.
Returns usable HTML or CSS the owner can paste back in, not only a description of what could be done.
